title: Pig butchering: following the money
body_md:
## Trace the money through the friendship

For weeks it is only a pleasant stranger who writes good morning and remembers what you said last Tuesday. Then, in passing, comes a mention of a trading app that has been doing well for them, and an offer to show you how it works.

This is confidence-based investment fraud: trust first, then a trading site or app presented as a shared opportunity. The site shows invented gains and may even let you withdraw a small sum. Later deposits grow, and a request to take everything out brings an invented tax, a fee or a frozen account. The FBI describes this sequence, though not every real case follows every step or timeline. A real friendship can also sit beside a real investment, so the test is who controls the money and what you can verify yourself, not whether someone is being warm.

Ask four separate questions: **Who introduced the platform? Who legally operates it? Where did your money actually go? Can you withdraw without sending new money that the published terms never mention?** The route often passes through a genuine exchange, which is why it reassures: you buy coins there, as instructed, then send them on to a wallet someone else controls. The exchange handled the purchase and vouched for nothing after it. A small withdrawal that does reach you proves just as little. The scammer can afford it, and it buys your trust for the larger deposits.

### If you, or someone close, is already in it

Pause new deposits at once. Do not “test” the site with a bigger withdrawal if getting it out means sending new money, handing identity documents over in the chat, or paying a fee. Ask someone you trust to look at the sequence with you, without blame. Keep private copies of the chats, site address, payment confirmations, wallet addresses and hashes, and do not post sensitive evidence in public. Contact the real bank, exchange or payment service quickly, and report to your local authority. In the US, IC3 takes complaints and transaction details, and no report promises recovery. Anyone who approaches you offering to recover the money for an advance fee is a second loss waiting to happen.

widget_config.goal: Spot the moment an online relationship is being turned into deposits on a platform someone else controls, and stop the money.
widget_config.today_action: Write yourself a three-line rule: no investment transfer on a new contact’s instruction; check the provider independently; ask someone you trust before any second deposit.
widget_config.scope: The FBI and IC3 describe patterns reported in the US. They are not a universal sequence, and no report guarantees recovery. The people and sites in the cases are invented. Checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Investment Fraud
sources.scope: How US law enforcement describes fake investment platforms built on trust.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Cryptocurrency
sources.scope: US reporting and transaction evidence. Blockchain transfers generally cannot be reversed.

sources.title: FTC: What To Do if You Were Scammed
sources.scope: US advice on payment providers and accounts. Recovery is not promised.

blocks.title: A winning screen after months of messages
blocks.situation: After months of friendly messages, a contact walks Maya through buying coins on a well-known exchange and sending them to harbor-yield.example. The site shows a profit and pays out a small amount. Now it suggests a much larger deposit.
blocks.analysis: The exchange handled only the purchase. It never vetted where the coins went next. The site controls the balance on the screen and can easily fund a small payout. Stop sending anything, find out independently who runs the site, and talk the sequence through with someone you trust.

blocks.title: A partner mentions an ordinary fund
blocks.situation: A long-term partner mentions a broad-market fund at a regulated provider. They do not touch the account or ask you to send anything. You open the provider’s site yourself and decide whether the risk suits you.
blocks.analysis: Advice from someone close is not coercion or fraud by default. Verify the provider and the exact product yourself, understand the losses and fees, and keep sole control of the account. A regulated account still guarantees no returns.

blocks.title: Helping a friend pause the deposits
blocks.setup: An invented scenario. Your friend Leon has been chatting with an online match who introduced him to north-chart.example. Leon has made two deposits and one small withdrawal.

steps.prompt: Leon says the withdrawal that went through proves the site is safe. How do you answer?

choices.text: Tell him he is being foolish and should admit it.
choices.consequence: He may pull away from you while the scammer stays persuasive.

choices.text: Explain calmly that a site someone controls can pay out a little to build trust.
choices.consequence: Leon gets a concrete reason to pause without feeling attacked.
choices.explanation: Skip the shame and explain the mechanism. Do not call him gullible.

steps.prompt: Leon plans to borrow money for another deposit. What is the first boundary?

choices.text: Deposit only half, to limit the risk.
choices.consequence: More money reaches a destination nobody has verified.
choices.explanation: A smaller amount is still exposure.

choices.text: Pause all new payments and any borrowing until the operator is verified.
choices.consequence: What he stands to lose stops growing.
choices.explanation: A pause can be lifted later. A new transfer may not be undone.

steps.prompt: The site now asks for a “tax” payment before Leon can withdraw. What should he do?

choices.text: Refuse to pay, contact the payment providers and keep the transaction records.
choices.consequence: He avoids a second loss, and the paper trail stays intact.
choices.explanation: A separate payment to release the money matches the pattern the FBI describes.

choices.text: Pay it, because the profit on screen is bigger.
choices.consequence: The screen can change. The new transfer is real.
choices.explanation: Never swap real money for a balance nobody has verified.

steps.prompt: What goes into a report, and how?

choices.text: Post account screenshots, personal details included, in public.
choices.consequence: Private details may reach the next scammer.
choices.explanation: A public post is no way to preserve evidence.

choices.text: Privately keep the site address, chats, dates, provider receipts and wallet addresses or hashes.
choices.consequence: A provider or an investigator can follow the trail step by step.
choices.explanation: Hand sensitive evidence over only through the real institution’s own channel.

blocks.debrief: The safe move is to stop the next transfer, support the person and preserve the payment trail. A small withdrawal is no certificate of legitimacy. Go back and try the answers you skipped.

blocks.title: Where trust turns into a deposit

questions.prompt: A real exchange sold you coins that you later sent to a stranger’s platform. What did the exchange validate?

choices.explanation: Processing a purchase is not an endorsement of outside wallets.

choices.text: Only its own purchase service, not the outside recipient.
choices.explanation: The final wallet is a separate decision about trust.

questions.prompt: A platform lets you make a small withdrawal. What is the sound conclusion?

choices.text: It can pay out a small sum, and that alone says little about the rest of the balance.
choices.explanation: A platform someone controls can use small payouts as bait.

choices.text: All the displayed profits are real.
choices.explanation: A number on a screen is no proof that anyone holds the assets.

questions.prompt: A friend who sent money is too embarrassed to tell anyone. What helps?

choices.text: Support a pause, keeping the evidence and contacting the provider, with no blame.
choices.explanation: That limits further loss and keeps the two of you talking.

choices.text: Warn them you will tell everyone if they do not listen.
choices.explanation: Shame pushes people further into isolation.
